title: The Questions Everyone Asks
description: "Where are you from?" "What do you do?" "Is Nepal safe?" You'll hear these a thousand times. Learn answers that are honest, a little funny, and easy to reply to.

vibe.setting: Cafe, first minute of a chat
vibe.scenario: A traveller asks you, "So where are you from?"

options.text: Right here — born two streets from the lake. I'm the souvenir you can't take home.
I'm from Pokhara. I was born here and I grew up here, and my family is also from here.

vibe.why: A plain fact plus one playful detail gives them something to laugh at and something to ask about.

options.text: Why do you want to know? That's a bit personal, no?
Officially, tourism. Unofficially, I'm the guy who knows where the best momos are.

vibe.why: The job answers the question. The "unofficial" part shows who you are and gives them an easy next question.

vibe.scenario: A first-time solo traveller asks seriously, "Is Nepal safe?"

options.text: Totally safe! Nothing ever happens here, you can do anything, go anywhere, anytime, no problem at all!
Generally, yes — people here look out for visitors. Use normal sense at night, and watch the traffic more than the people.

vibe.why: A serious question deserves a real answer. Honest and reassuring beats a promise you can't keep.

vibe.scenario: A tourist grins: "Have you ever climbed Everest?"

options.text: Only in my dreams — and even there I needed oxygen.
No. Not every Nepali climbs Everest, you know. That's a stereotype, and honestly it's a bit annoying.

vibe.why: They're not being rude, just curious. A joke keeps it warm; a lecture makes them regret asking.

vibe.scenario: A traveller asks, "What's your favourite place in Nepal?"

options.text: Everywhere is nice. I don't really have one.
A tiny teahouse above Ghandruk where the owner sings while she cooks. The mountains are a bonus.
Pokhara, but also Kathmandu, and Chitwan, and Mustang, and Ilam… there are so many, it's hard to choose.

vibe.why: One small, real detail makes your answer a story. Use your own real place — the specific detail is what matters.

vibe.scenario: A traveller asks, "Do you speak Hindi?"

options.text: Enough to follow a Bollywood film and guess the villain early. Nepali is my first language, though.
Nepali and Hindi are totally different languages, you know. We're not India.

vibe.why: You answered honestly, cleared up the mix-up gently, and gave them a smile.

vibe.scenario: An older traveller asks casually, "How old are you?"

options.text: Old enough to know the best momo shop, young enough to still eat twenty.
I'm twenty-eight. My birthday is in March, so almost twenty-nine, actually.

vibe.why: You can answer or dodge, but do it warmly. In many cultures this question is just friendly.

options.text: No, I'm not married. Not yet. Maybe in a few years, I don't know, we'll see what happens.
Not yet. My mother reminds me every day, so please don't join her team.

vibe.why: A small, true detail about your family makes you human and funny. Flirting back at a general question is a gamble.

vibe.scenario: A traveller asks, "What should I eat in Nepal?"

options.text: Dal bhat for power, momos for joy, and sel roti if you catch a festival. In that order.
Whatever. Everything here is spicy anyway, so it doesn't really matter what you order.

vibe.why: Three items, each with a reason, is a rhythm people remember. It sounds like advice from a friend.

vibe.scenario: A new arrival asks, "Why does everyone say 'namaste' to me?"

options.text: It means hello. You can say it anytime — morning, afternoon, evening. It's like "hi", but for everything.
It's hello with extra respect. Say it back with your hands together and watch people's faces light up.

vibe.why: You explained it and gave them a small action. Now they'll try it, and it'll work.

vibe.scenario: A traveller asks, "Do you like living here?"

options.text: No, I want to leave. There are no jobs, nothing works, everyone my age wants to go abroad.
Most days, yes. The traffic, no. The view from my window, always.

vibe.why: Real life has good and bad. Three short beats show both, and end on the good.

vibe.scenario: A traveller asks, "Can you recommend a trekking guide?"

options.text: Me! I'm the best. Special price for you, we can go tomorrow, I promise you won't regret it!
I can give you two names I trust. Meet both, and pick the one who laughs at your jokes — you'll be together for ten days.

vibe.why: Giving them a choice builds trust. People remember the local who helped, not the one who pushed.

cards.text: Pokhara, born and raised. What about you — where's home, and do you miss it yet?
cards.why: Answers, then asks two easy questions back.

yesAnd.prompt: Do you get tired of tourists?

cards.text: Only the ones who skip the momos. You're safe so far — what have you tried?
cards.why: A friendly joke that includes them, then a question.
Honest, but now they feel like a burden.

cards.text: No, visas are hard for us.
cards.why: True and important, but it ends the chat on a low note.

cards.text: Not yet — so tell me about yours. What's one thing I'd find really weird there?
cards.why: Turns it into a fun question about their world.

yesAnd.prompt: What's the best time to visit Nepal?

cards.text: Autumn for clear mountains, spring for flowers. Honestly, whenever you're here is the best time. How long are you staying?
cards.why: Useful, warm, and a question to keep it going.

yesAnd.prompt: Is it rude to eat with my left hand?

cards.why: Makes them nervous and gives no help.

cards.text: Traditionally the right hand is for eating, but people will forgive you. Want to try dal bhat the local way?
cards.why: Honest, relaxed, and an invitation to learn.

yesAnd.prompt: What do Nepali people do for fun?

cards.text: Tea, cards, gossip, and more tea. Want to see a real Nepali card game? Warning: we get loud.
cards.why: A funny list, then a real invitation.
Nothing for them to hold on to.

yesAnd.prompt: Why is the music on the buses so loud?

cards.text: It keeps the driver awake and the passengers entertained. By hour three you'll know every song. Got a favourite yet?
cards.why: A funny explanation and a question they'll laugh at.

cards.text: I don't know, they just do.

yesAnd.prompt: How do you say 'delicious' in Nepali?

cards.why: Correct, but you stopped at the dictionary.

cards.text: "Mitho!" Say it to the cook and you might get a second plate. Try it on me first — say it like you mean it.
cards.why: Teaches the word, gives a reason to use it, and invites them to practise.

upgrader.clunky: I am, um, from Nepal, from Pokhara, here only, like.
upgrader.why: One place, one detail. The detail is what makes them ask more.

upgrader.clunky: I work in, like, tourism, so, many things, guiding, some cafe, like that.
upgrader.why: Give your job a shape: what you do, and when. It sounds organised and interesting.

upgrader.clunky: Nepal is safe, very safe, no problem, very very safe.
upgrader.why: Say it once, then add one honest detail. The detail makes the reassurance believable.

upgrader.clunky: The best time is, maybe, October, November, because the weather is, like, clear.
upgrader.why: Start with the answer as an invitation ("Come in…"), then give the reason as a picture.

upgrader.clunky: I don't know, many foods are good, dal bhat also, momo also.
upgrader.why: An order ("start with… then…") sounds like expert advice.

upgrader.clunky: No, I did not climb Everest, it is very expensive and very difficult.
upgrader.why: "Not yet" is more fun than "no". The ending turns a fact into a joke.

upgrader.clunky: Yes, I like living here, it is good, nice, peaceful, good.
upgrader.why: Three short pictures in a row have rhythm. Much better than repeating "good".

upgrader.clunky: Namaste means, like, hello, but also, um, respect, something like that.
upgrader.why: One clean definition. No hedging needed — you know this better than they do.

dropIn.fact: Dal bhat — rice, lentil soup, vegetables and pickle — is Nepal's everyday meal. Teahouses on trekking routes usually give free refills.
dropIn.source: Nepal Tourism Board; common teahouse practice on trekking routes
dropIn.prompt: A trekker asks, "Why does everyone here eat dal bhat every day?"

options.text: Because it's cheap and people don't have money for other food.
options.why: Reduces a much-loved meal to poverty. Not the full story, and not kind.

options.text: Because it's the only meal with free refills and its own slogan — "dal bhat power, 24 hour". Try it on day one of the trek.
options.why: Fun, true, and it makes them want to try it.

options.text: Dal bhat is the national everyday meal, and refills are usually free.
options.why: Accurate, a bit like a guidebook.

dropIn.fact: "Namaste" comes from Sanskrit and means roughly "I bow to you".
dropIn.prompt: A traveller asks, "What does namaste actually mean?"

options.why: Sells short something beautiful.
Correct, but it stops before the good part.

options.text: Roughly "I bow to you". So every time you say it, you're being quietly very polite — and people notice.
options.why: Meaning plus why it matters to them.

dropIn.fact: October and November usually have the clearest mountain views in Nepal, after the monsoon clears the air. Spring is the second-best season.
dropIn.prompt: A traveller asks, "When's the best time to see the mountains?"

options.why: It really does matter, and they asked you for a reason.

options.text: October and November — the monsoon washes the sky clean. Spring comes second, with rhododendrons as the prize.
options.why: Clear answer, a picture, and a bonus tip.

options.text: October and November are usually the best months, because the monsoon rain is finished and the air is clean, so the views are clear.
options.why: Correct and complete, but long and flat — no picture, no bonus.

dropIn.fact: Nepali is written in the Devanagari script, the same alphabet used for Hindi.
dropIn.prompt: A traveller points at a shop sign: "Is that Hindi?"

options.text: Same alphabet, different language. It's Nepali — like Spanish and Italian sharing one alphabet.
options.why: Corrects gently with a comparison they understand.

options.text: No! It's Nepali. Everyone mixes that up and it's so annoying.
options.why: Makes them feel stupid for a normal mistake.

options.text: No, it's Nepali, written in the Devanagari script.
options.why: Correct, but "Devanagari" alone won't help them.

dropIn.fact: Nepal's 2021 census counted about 29 million people.
dropIn.source: National Statistics Office, Nepal, "National Population and Housing Census 2021"
dropIn.prompt: A traveller asks, "How many people live in Nepal?"

options.why: You could have been interesting here.

options.text: About 29 million at the last census — and every one of them has an opinion on the best momo shop.
options.why: The number, plus a joke that makes it human.

options.text: About 29 million people, according to the national census in 2021. Most of them live in the Terai and the hills.
options.why: Accurate, but lots of information and no fun.

dropIn.fact: In Nepal it's polite to give and receive money, food and gifts with your right hand, or with both hands for extra respect.
dropIn.prompt: A traveller hands money to an old shopkeeper with their left hand. The shopkeeper frowns a little.

options.why: Dramatic and embarrassing. It won't help next time.

options.text: Quick local tip: give money with your right hand — or both hands for extra respect. Watch the smiles change.
options.why: Quiet, useful, and it promises a nice result.

options.text: In Nepal you should always use your right hand to give money, because the left hand is traditionally seen as unclean here.
options.why: Helpful, but loud and a bit embarrassing for them in front of the shopkeeper.
Strong and common. It makes people curious.
Good word, but less common in speech.
Now it sounds boring.

wordPower.example: Talking to people from forty countries a week is fascinating.

wordPower.sentence: Pokhara is a very relaxing place.

options.why: Beautiful but a little formal.
Relaxing is not the same as boring.
Casual, friendly, and exactly the vibe.

wordPower.example: Lakeside has a laid-back feel, even in high season.

wordPower.sentence: The people in my village are very friendly.

options.why: Says they open their homes, not just smile.
Weaker than "very friendly".
Correct, but a bit formal for chat.

wordPower.meaning: Making you feel at home right away.
wordPower.example: The family at the homestay was so welcoming.

wordPower.sentence: Dal bhat gives you a lot of energy.
wordPower.target: gives you a lot of energy

options.why: True, but a different point.
Everyday English that paints a picture.
Sounds like an advert for an energy drink.

wordPower.meaning: Gives you energy for a long time.
wordPower.example: A strong tea at six keeps me going till noon.

wordPower.sentence: Kathmandu is very crowded and busy.

options.why: Honest and positive at the same time.
The opposite.
Correct, but hard words that many travellers won't know.

wordPower.meaning: Very busy and a bit crazy, but enjoyable.
wordPower.example: Asan market is chaotic in a fun way.

wordPower.sentence: In July it rains very heavily here.

options.why: Means light rain. Wrong direction.
Weather-report English, not conversation.
One short word. Everyone understands.

wordPower.example: It pours every afternoon in the monsoon.

wordPower.sentence: Everest is a very famous mountain.

options.why: Correct, a bit formal.
Famous plus stories. It fits Everest.
Weaker than famous.

wordPower.meaning: Very famous, with stories told about it.
wordPower.example: The momos at that little shop are legendary.

wordPower.sentence: I was very surprised when I saw the price.

options.why: Clear, strong and common.
A different feeling.
Fun word, but many learners won't know it.

wordPower.meaning: Very surprised, often in a bad way.
wordPower.example: I was shocked at how cheap the fruit was.
